title: Can you crack 1101 by trying keys?
hook: You intercept a 4-bit secret and can try every key. Does that tell you the message?

doesNotKnow: that XOR with a random key used once hides the message completely

misconception: If you try all keys, the one that gives a sensible message reveals the message.
objective: The learner can explain that the ciphertext 1101 fits all 16 possible 4-bit messages, each with its own key, so trying keys cannot single out the message.

claims.text: XOR gives 1 where the two bits differ.
claims.source: Truth table of exclusive OR (e.g. Harris and Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture, 1.5).

claims.text: For every 4-bit message there is a key that turns it into 1101: the key is the message XOR 1101.
claims.source: (m XOR k) = c iff k = m XOR c, since XOR is its own inverse. Demo.tsx keyFor(m) = m ^ CIPHER; the stage shows m XOR key = 1101.

claims.text: All 16 possible 4-bit messages fit 1101, and all 16 keys are different.
claims.source: Node: new Set([...Array(16)].map((_, m) => m ^ 0b1101)).size = 16. Demo.tsx DISTINCT_KEYS.

claims.text: If the key was random, every message is equally likely given 1101, so trying keys only lists every message.
claims.source: Perfect secrecy of the one-time pad with a uniformly random key: C. E. Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems', Bell System Technical Journal 28(4), 1949. Here: each message maps to exactly one of the 16 equally likely keys.

claims.text: This is a one-time pad, and it stays unbreakable only if the key is never used again.
claims.source: Reuse leaks: c1 XOR c2 = (m1 XOR k) XOR (m2 XOR k) = m1 XOR m2. Name: Vernam (1919 patent) / Mauborgne; Shannon 1949. 'Unbreakable' is meant as perfect secrecy against key search, assuming a truly random, secret key.

recall.question: A 3-bit message was XORed with a random 3-bit key used once. You see the result. How many 3-bit messages could it be?
recall.why: Every one of the 8 messages has its own key that gives the same result (key = message XOR result), so none is ruled out.
